item.title: WSL talking points: pressure mounts on Slegers as Hemp closes on record
item.description: Another round of games and another disappointing draw for Arsenal while Manchester City sit top of the table with a 100% record There would have been hope that the international break could offer the Arsenal players and staff a reset but the same problems reared their head at the Emirates on Sunday in a 1-1 draw with Birmingham. As they have done so often this season, the Gunners dominated most attacking and possession-based metrics – they registered 76% possession, a 2.73 xG and 43 touches in the opposition box – but their profligacy in front of goal and lack of urgency in their play once again came to the fore. Of their 27 chances, they managed just four on target as they toiled against a resilient opposition who understood the playbook. Birmingham set up in a strong defensive structure, protecting their box admirably with numbers to frustrate Renée Slegers’s side, who famously struggle to break down low blocks. In contrast, Birmingham scored with their one shot on target as Océane Hurtré took her impressive tally to six in six. Sophie Downey Match report: Arsenal 1-1 Birmingham Continue reading...

item.title: Les Misérables: Macron's 'sense of detachment' amid rising living costs and youth 'fears for future'
item.description: France’s escalating protest movement is exposing a widening disconnect between political leadership and public frustration, while raising questions about the country’s long tradition of social unrest. Chris Reynolds, Professor of French and European Studies at Nottingham Trent University, argues that President Emmanuel Macron’s latest address was characterised by a troubling “sense of detachment,” offering little to resolve the structural grievances driving the demonstrations. Drawing parallels with May 1968 and the Yellow Vest movement, Reynolds warns that violent unrest risks eclipsing the legitimate concerns of largely peaceful protesters, undermining public sympathy and reshaping political debate ahead of the presidential election.

item.title: 5 New Music Videos You Need to Watch This Week: Victony, Tyla, Phyno & More
item.description: Nigerian singer-songwriter Victony wearing a glossy leather outfit on set during the production of the SLICK Remix, featuring American stars Don Toliver and Summer Walker, off his sophomore album STARLIFE. A new week calls for fresh music, and there’s plenty to add to your watchlist. From Victony bringing Don Toliver and Summer Walker into the mix for the “ SLICK ” remix to Tyla ’s dance-ready “ That Girl ” and Phyno ’s romantic “Beautiful”, there’s something for every mood. We’re also looking back at Ayra Starr ’s performance at the 2026 NFL international halftime show and making room for Anendlessocean ’s reflective “ Promises ”. Here are five music releases and performances to check out this week. Victony: “SLICK (Remix)” ft. Don Toliver & Summer Walker Victony has given “SLICK” a new twist, and this time, he’s brought Don Toliver and Summer Walker along for the ride. The original track appears on his sophomore album, STARLIFE, while the remix introduces a fresh mix of R&B vocals and melodies. With three artistes bringing their different sounds to the same record, there’s plenty to enjoy here. Tyla: “That Girl” If you’re looking for something to get you moving, Tyla has you covered with “That Girl” from her project A*Pop. The song draws on South Africa’s popular Phara Walk dance culture, pairing catchy rhythms with Tyla’s smooth vocals. It’s playful, danceable and one you might find yourself returning to throughout the week. Anendlessocean: “Promises” Anendlessocean offers a place for reflection, gratitude and rest with “Promises”. Rooted in faith and the assurance that God will come through again, the song invites listeners to pause, reflect and find comfort in the belief that He will do it again. It’s one to turn to when you need a little reminder to trust the journey. Phyno: “Beautiful” Ezege is back with “Beautiful”, a love letter to the woman who makes everything make sense. Smooth, heartfelt and unmistakably Phyno, the track blends Igbo, Pidgin and English over a melody made for the ones you hold close. Taken from his project Let That Sink In (LTSI), the song celebrates love in a way that feels personal and familiar. The official music video features actress and media personality Nancy Isime, giving the romantic track a visual companion. Ayra Starr: 2026 NFL Halftime Performance Ayra Starr took Afrobeats to the NFL international stage on 11 October, headlining the halftime show during the Philadelphia Eagles vs Jacksonville Jaguars game at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium in London. She opened her set with “Heaven Baby”, her collaboration with ZAYN, before performing “Santa”, “Rush” and “Dangerous”, and closing with a medley of “Hot Body” and “Ms. Paper”. The performance marked a major milestone for the Nigerian star, who became the first African artiste to headline an NFL International Games halftime show. item.title: Museum exhibit reveals the intricate workings of a knackered Dell
item.description: Today's entry in the catalog of bork comes from Coventry's Herbert Art Gallery & Museum, where an information terminal is showing more about the hardware behind the scenes than the objects on display. Register reader Jeffrey Borinsky spotted the panel, which should have demonstrated a Jacquard loom in action but was instead displaying a warning about its host PC's failing battery. The Jacquard loom was a clever device dating back to the dawn of the 19th century. It used punched cards to control a loom's weaving patterns. The result was complicated and repeatable textile designs that reduced the need for skilled humans. Register readers of a certain age are doubtless nodding sagely at the mention of punched cards, which would go on to become foundational in the world of computing. Borinsky reported that several screens at the museum were in distress. Ribbon weaving was Coventry's main industry from the early 1700s until the 1860s, so a demonstration of Jacquard weaving fits right in, even if the bleating about the BIOS battery was probably not what Joseph Jacquard had in mind. The device running behind the scenes is a Dell OptiPlex 755, likely from around 2007. Not quite centuries old like a Jacquard loom, but certainly getting on a bit in the IT world. The first iPhone arrived in 2007, and a PC of a similar vintage likely shipped with Windows XP or Windows Vista. The CMOS battery is on the way out. Dell specifies a CR2032 coin cell, so replacement should be straightforward after disconnecting the power and taking anti-static precautions. Rather less traumatic than the head-in-hands moment when a retro enthusiast discovers a leaking battery has eaten through delicate circuit traces. A fresh battery and restored BIOS settings should be enough to get the loom demonstration weaving again. Given how important punched cards became in the history of computing, we'd recommend visiting anywhere that shows how a Jacquard loom operated. At least it didn't need a battery-backed BIOS to do its thing. ®

item.title: French interior minister admits police 'lost control' of protests
item.description: France's Interior Minister Laurent Nunez admitted Monday that the police "lost control" in some cities during violent protests that erupted in cities across the country at the weekend. Macron did not accept his resignation.

Her deal was due to expire after next summer’s World Cup and this gives her the chance to lead the Lionesses to three European championship titles in a row. Wiegman, who took on the role in September 2021 , also led her native Netherlands to Euros glory in 2017 and has reached the final of the past five major tournaments, twice finishing as a World Cup runner-up. item.title: Watch Japan launch a bold sample-return mission to Mars moon Phobos today
item.description: null Japan will launch an epic mission to Mars today (Oct. 19), and you can watch the action live. The Martian Moons eXploration ( MMX ) mission is scheduled to lift off atop an H3 rocket from Japan's Tanegashima Space Center today at 3:41 p.m. EDT (1941 GMT; 4:41 a.m. on Oct. 20 local Japan time). You can watch it live via the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA). Coverage will begin at 2:45 p.m. EDT (1845 GMT). An artist’s concept of JAXA’s MMX spacecraft during its Mars orbit insertion. The Martian moon Phobos, which MMX will explore and sample, is in the background. (Image credit: JAXA) As its full name suggests, MMX will focus on Mars ' two moons, Phobos and Deimos . They're both tiny compared to Earth's own moon; Phobos is just 14 miles (22 kilometers) wide, and Deimos is even smaller, with a diameter of about 8 miles (13 km). They're also quite mysterious. While astronomers have a pretty clear understanding of our own moon's birth — it coalesced from material blasted into space when a Mars-sized planet slammed into Earth long ago — there's no consensus about Phobos and Deimos' origin story. The duo "may be the remains of a massive impact on Mars that sent material into orbit around the planet, or they could be ancient asteroids that were captured by Mars' gravity billions of years ago," Tom Statler, MMX program executive and program scientist at NASA Headquarters, said in an Oct. 15 statement . (NASA is a partner on the mission, providing a scientific instrument, a technology demonstration, communication support and funding for American scientists on the MMX team.) "Having the answer will help illuminate that early era when Earth and the other inner planets may have been acquiring much of their water and organic compounds," Statler added. MMX will help provide that answer, if all goes according to plan. The spacecraft will arrive in the Mars system in August 2027, then slip into orbit around Phobos a month later. It will study that moon and Deimos from a distance for about 18 months, then deploy the French-German Idefix rover onto Phobos' surface in early 2029. The 55-pound (25 kilograms) Idefix "has two main tasks: providing information to prepare for the landing of the main spacecraft to collect samples, and analyzing the composition and texture of Phobos' surface," European Space Agency officials wrote in an MMX mission description . "The gravity on Phobos is so low that Idefix will only weigh the equivalent of 15 grams [0.5 ounces] on its surface!" they added. The MMX mothership's Phobos landing will occur in 2030. The spacecraft will grab at least 10 grams (0.4 ounces) of samples from the moon, then head back toward Earth with this extraterrestrial bounty. MMX's return capsule will land here in 2031, after which scientists around the world will scrutinize the Phobos sample for clues about the history and evolution of Mars and our solar system more broadly. Engineers conduct a thermal vacuum test with JAXA's MMX Mars moon sample-return spacecraft. JAXA posted this image on X on May 15, 2025. (Image credit: JAXA) MMX was originally supposed to launch in 2024, but issues with the H3 rocket prevented it from doing so. Mars and Earth align properly for interplanetary launches just once every 26 months, so MMX had to wait a while for its next chance. Japan already has an impressive sample-return track record. The country's Hayabusa mission brought home pieces of the asteroid Itokawa in 2010, for example, and Hayabusa2 did the same with material from the space rock Ryugu a decade later.

item.title: Microsoft’s second-hand licensing appeal gets the brush-off
item.description: Microsoft has failed to win permission to appeal to the UK Supreme Court in the long-running legal spat with ValueLicensing after the Court of Appeal refused its application. The US megacorp was challenging a November 2025 ruling in ValueLicensing's favor that VL may resell pre-owned software licenses. That judgment was unambiguous, but Microsoft told The Register at the time that it would seek permission to appeal. That request was rejected last week in blunt terms. No reasons were given for the refusal, just the words "It is ordered that the application is refused." It isn't quite the end of the road. Microsoft could apply to the Supreme Court itself, but it would need to file within 28 days and show a compelling reason why the Court of Appeal was wrong to refuse its appeal. Things are looking dicey for Microsoft in the case that started in 2021 when ValueLicensing sued Microsoft for £270 million over claims that the Windows maker choked off the supply of surplus Office licenses. Microsoft denied any wrongdoing and Instead attempted to reframe the case as a copyright dispute. The UK's Competition Appeal Tribunal rejected Microsoft's arguments and a subsequent appeal. A recently published Consent Order adds to the pressure. It demands documents from past and present Microsoft bosses, including a potentially explosive internal deck titled "Second-Hand Software Presentation" (SHS). The contents of the file are unknown, but the Consent Order refers to it as a "Known Adverse Document." It dates back to 2013, a few years after Office 365 was launched. The order also asks why Microsoft waited until the end of 2025 to disclose the document’s existence, a few years after Office 365 launched. To add a little more spice, Alexander Wolfson is listed as an intervener on the appeal refusal. He is the proposed class representative in a separate claim filed on behalf of millions of UK customers seeking between £1.3 billion to £3.5 billion in compensation from Microsoft over its conduct regarding pre-owned licenses. ValueLicensing and Microsoft declined to comment on the latest development. Appeals aside, the next stage will be a Witness Statement from Microsoft explaining who knew what and when, followed by further disclosure. ®

item.title: AI’s epic cash call is matched only by its ability to strangle revenue streams
item.description: As it was written, so it has come to pass. A while back, we suggested that given how good AI was at code analysis, it would become possible to clone large applications. And then where would we be? Here, that’s where. An industrious individual has released source code and binaries for Claude-copied Microsoft Office and Adobe Creative Suite programs, disappointingly not calling elements of the latter Fauxtoshop. They’re in pre-alpha states of incomplete bugginess, but with substantial functionality, which is proof of how insanely productive AI can be given a task needing zero creativity and wearing "This is what a proof of concept looks like" and "Unintended Consquesences" T-shirts. They could also add Karma Police to their wardrobe. It’s clear that Microsoft and Adobe are facing some competition from what their rival describes as "clean-room reimplementations." It’s also unclear that there is any law against it. You can’t copyright functionality, the code has been generated in Rust with claimed clean-room conditions, and while there may be something in claiming that the works are substantially derivative, there’s a big problem here. Companies that sell AI trained on the biggest theft of IP in history are going to need unmatched legal dexterity to claim that AI shouldn’t be allowed to sully their own IP. Chutzpah used to be defined as a child on trial for murdering their parents begging for mercy on the grounds that they’re an orphan. We’ll have to update that. The post-codeclone world is going to be interesting. Everything becomes effectively open source, which closes down substantial revenue streams for big companies who had assumed lock-in. The motivation to build ab-initio alternatives may go away, in open source as well as closed. The push to subscription-only cloud-hosted products, where nobody can get their thieving AI prompts on binaries, seems an obvious counter move, but AI can control and scrape a web interface, which is all it needs. It's an arms race that won’t be won by humans. Code cloning is just the latest case of AI being so disruptive it threatens its creators. Another is the doom loop that Microsoft-OpenAI acknowledged in internal emails: by siphoning away the ad revenue that pays for content, AI chokes off the data it depends on. It's deforestation by companies that built their business on other people's IP. The biggest potential point of failure is the money. How revenues will hold up against cheaper or free Chinese models is a concern, given the high importance assigned by Beijing to develop AI as a global influence vector. The models themselves are very efficient, in part because of export regulations on high-end silicon and something of a glut of older datacenters. This wouldn’t be the first time restricting access to technology is an evolutionary driver with a poor outcome for those doing the restricting. A much bigger issue is: where will the money come from to build the infrastructure that is needed to support the claims

And then where would we be? Here, that’s where. An industrious individual has released source code and binaries for Claude-copied Microsoft Office and Adobe Creative Suite programs, disappointingly not calling elements of the latter Fauxtoshop. They’re in pre-alpha states of incomplete bugginess, but with substantial functionality, which is proof of how insanely productive AI can be given a task needing zero creativity and wearing "This is what a proof of concept looks like" and "Unintended Consquesences" T-shirts. They could also add Karma Police to their wardrobe. It’s clear that Microsoft and Adobe are facing some competition from what their rival describes as "clean-room reimplementations." It’s also unclear that there is any law against it. You can’t copyright functionality, the code has been generated in Rust with claimed clean-room conditions, and while there may be something in claiming that the works are substantially derivative, there’s a big problem here. Companies that sell AI trained on the biggest theft of IP in history are going to need unmatched legal dexterity to claim that AI shouldn’t be allowed to sully their own IP. Chutzpah used to be defined as a child on trial for murdering their parents begging for mercy on the grounds that they’re an orphan. We’ll have to update that. The post-codeclone world is going to be interesting. Everything becomes effectively open source, which closes down substantial revenue streams for big companies who had assumed lock-in. The motivation to build ab-initio alternatives may go away, in open source as well as closed. The push to subscription-only cloud-hosted products, where nobody can get their thieving AI prompts on binaries, seems an obvious counter move, but AI can control and scrape a web interface, which is all it needs. It's an arms race that won’t be won by humans. Code cloning is just the latest case of AI being so disruptive it threatens its creators. Another is the doom loop that Microsoft-OpenAI acknowledged in internal emails: by siphoning away the ad revenue that pays for content, AI chokes off the data it depends on. It's deforestation by companies that built their business on other people's IP. The biggest potential point of failure is the money. How revenues will hold up against cheaper or free Chinese models is a concern, given the high importance assigned by Beijing to develop AI as a global influence vector. The models themselves are very efficient, in part because of export regulations on high-end silicon and something of a glut of older datacenters. This wouldn’t be the first time restricting access to technology is an evolutionary driver with a poor outcome for those doing the restricting. A much bigger issue is: where will the money come from to build the infrastructure that is needed to support the claims AI is using to justify its growth. Gartner says that there’s not enough return on investment to drive that growth, while a much more engaging SemiAnalysis podcast predicts total capex by 2030 of $11 trillion and asks where it’s going to come from. If you’re interested in understanding AI and aren't following SemiAnalysis, you’re not interested in understanding AI, and while the outfit is relentlessly optimistic it’s also wildly well-informed. In this case, the structure of the investment market for AI is picked apart. It is very weird. Neocloud is made up of startups with a voracious appetite for cash, but no investment grade status. Thus, Nvidia backstops them, guaranteeing to rent unsold capacity for a fixed price for long enough to guarantee enough revenue to attract other investment. Other cash-rich big tech companies do similar things. This backstopping, also known more wryly as "balance sheet as a service," effectively shifts more risk to investment-rated companies. It's an increasingly important capex enabler, but as SemiAnalysis says, it’s necessarily limited, especially if AI itself has blown a hole in the enterprise. Or take the residual value of the older compute. Normally, the book value and revenue capabilities of datacenter chips depreciates over five years or so to some nominal value. That’s not happening here, where chips of that vintage are suddenly producing the same or more revenue than they did when they were new. Such are the peculiarities of a supply-constrained market used to rapid obsolescence. Surely a good thing, though? No. It’s another strange and hard-to-model factor in a market defined by strange and hard-to-model factors. Don’t even mention AGI. Or models too dangerous to use. Or model collapse. Many investors do not like the strange and hard to model, including huge pools of institutional funds. There are models that can blend in risk-averse investors to speculative investments, but those who remember the clever models that blew up the global economy nearly twenty years ago are not yet all dead. The tl;dr of the answer to where do you get enough money to make AI work as promised, is: nobody knows. What happens if the capex has no cap to ex? See previous answer. It may be an infantile affliction to have animation clips come to mind when considering AI, but it can’t be helped. Agentic AI? Mickey Mouse as the sorcerer's apprentice in Fantasia. Big Tech pushing out AI as fast as it can? Wile E Coyote sawing through the branch he’s sitting on. AI investment market? Any of Caine’s quests in the Amazing Digital Circus. We’re all along for the ride, whether we like it or not. ®

item.title: AI inference is running into a memory bottleneck. Huawei wants to tackle it with OceanStor M900
item.description: As organizations move from straightforward AI interactions towards longer conversations, complex reasoning and autonomous agents, the demands on their infrastructure are changing. Processing increasingly large amounts of context places significant pressure on memory capacity, while keeping accelerators supplied with data becomes just as important as raw computing power. One particular challenge is the key-value (KV) cache, which stores information generated during inference so models can reuse previous computations rather than repeatedly processing the same context. As context windows expand and multi-turn interactions become more demanding, these caches grow considerably. GPU memory and system memory provide fast access but are expensive and capacity constrained. Traditional storage offers greater capacity, yet its longer, CPU-mediated data paths can introduce latency that leaves valuable accelerator resources waiting for data. Huawei believes addressing this gap requires a different approach to storage. Bringing context memory closer to compute At HUAWEI CONNECT 2026 in Shanghai, Huawei introduced OceanStor M900 Context Memory Storage, designed to support AI inference across hyperscale datacenters and its Ascend SuperPoD infrastructure. The platform introduces what Huawei describes as a dedicated Context Memory Storage layer, extending KV cache beyond accelerator and system memory into a shared, multi-tier storage pool. Using Huawei's UnifiedBus high-speed interconnect, OceanStor M900 enables KV cache resources to be shared across a cluster, with Huawei claiming capacity of up to 64PB and substantially more context available per NPU. Its innovative ASU disk also integrates CPU, networking and storage controller functions. Combined with native KV semantics, this allows NPUs to access stored cache data in a single hop, avoiding conventional protocol conversion and CPU forwarding. According to Huawei, this approach reduces access latency to 60 microseconds, potentially doubling token throughput and halving time to first token in typical AI coding workloads. Cost and durability are also part of the proposition. Huawei's KV-aware adaptive storage technology manages data placement according to cache lifecycles, with claimed endurance of up to 24 drive writes per day, or 16 times that of conventional SSDs. The company argues this could reduce replacement and maintenance costs over time. The wider significance of OceanStor M900 lies in Huawei's approach to AI infrastructure. Rather than treating storage as a separate supporting component, the company is positioning memory, networking and compute as increasingly interconnected elements of inference performance. As agentic AI workloads grow, how efficiently infrastructure retains, shares and retrieves context may become as important as how quickly its accelerators can process it. Sponsored by Huawei

item.title: Farmers-herders violence in FCT
item.description: T hree people have been reportedly killed and several others injured in a renewed farmers-herders clash in Paikon-Kore community, Gwagwalada Area Council of the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), with houses and a motorcycle reportedly set ablaze. The violence, which began on Saturday afternoon and continued until Sunday morning, also left several shops at the Paikon-Kore village market burnt and goods destroyed. Experts urge that there is a need to nip the brewing crisis in the bud to avoid recurring deadly scenarios witnessed in other states like Benue and Plateau states, where farmers-herders clashes have claimed hundreds of lives and displaced many. A resident of the community, Danlami Ibrahim, said the clash started after some herders allegedly allowed their cattle into a groundnut farm whose crops were yet to be harvested. Rainbow coalition stirs more controversies in states Dangote Refinery IPO attracts investors from 90 countries He said the farm owner confronted the herders over the intrusion, triggering a heated argument. According to him, one of the herders allegedly brought out a cutlass and attacked a farmer, severing one of his hands. Ibrahim said the incident sparked anger among residents, particularly after other community members learnt of the farmer’s injury, leading to a reprisal in which three herders were reportedly killed. He added that two houses, several shops and a motorcycle were set ablaze during the violence. The resident said the clash continued until Sunday morning, leaving several people injured. Some of the victims were subsequently taken to hospitals in Gwagwalada for treatment. A visit to the affected village market by our correspondent showed several wooden, zinc-built and container shops burnt, with smoke still billowing from some of the shops. At Sabon Nakowa Hospital, a private medical facility in Gwagwalada, some victims were seen receiving treatment. item.content:encoded: T hree people have been reportedly killed and several others injured in a renewed farmers-herders clash in Paikon-Kore community, Gwagwalada Area Council of the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), with houses and a motorcycle reportedly set ablaze. The violence, which began on Saturday afternoon and continued until Sunday morning, also left several shops at the Paikon-Kore village market burnt and goods destroyed. Experts urge that there is a need to nip the brewing crisis in the bud to avoid recurring deadly scenarios witnessed in other states like Benue and Plateau states, where farmers-herders clashes have claimed hundreds of lives and displaced many. A resident of the community, Danlami Ibrahim, said the clash started after some herders allegedly allowed their cattle into a groundnut farm whose crops were yet to be harvested. Rainbow coalition stirs more controversies in states Dangote Refinery IPO attracts investors from 90 countries He said the farm owner confronted the herders over the intrusion, triggering a heated argument. According to him, one of the herders allegedly brought out a cutlass and attacked a farmer, severing one of his hands. Ibrahim said the incident sparked anger among residents, particularly after other community members learnt of the farmer’s injury, leading to a reprisal in which three herders were reportedly killed. He added that two houses, several shops and a motorcycle were set ablaze during the violence. The resident said the clash continued until Sunday morning, leaving several people injured. Some of the victims were subsequently taken to hospitals in Gwagwalada for treatment. A visit to the affected village market by our correspondent showed several wooden, zinc-built and container shops burnt, with smoke still billowing from some of the shops. At Sabon Nakowa Hospital, a private medical facility in Gwagwalada, some victims were seen receiving treatment. Two others were also observed undergoing treatment at the accident and emergency unit of the University of Abuja Teaching Hospital. The Secretary of the Miyetti Allah Cattle Breeders Association of Nigeria (MACBAN), Gwagwalada Area Council chapter, Mohammed Usman, said three herders lost their lives. “For now, information at my disposal shows that three herders lost their lives. That is what I can say for now, while I am yet to get the number of those who sustained injuries,” he said. Usman said he would provide further information as it became available, adding that he had informed the Gwagwalada Area Council chairman, Kasim Mohammed Ikwa, about the incident. Ikwa, who visited the affected community on Sunday alongside the Divisional Police Officer, SP Aaron H. Kaura, and other security operatives, condemned the renewed violence, describing it as unfortunate. He said the council would convene a stakeholders’ meeting on Monday (today) to deliberate on the crisis and seek ways to prevent further violence. The chairman urged both warring parties to embrace peace and avoid actions capable of escalating tensions. He also called on youths in Paikon-Kore to exercise restraint and promote peaceful coexistence with other residents, warning against confrontation and retaliatory attacks. Ikwa advised farmers whose crops were damaged by cattle to report such incidents to the relevant security agencies rather than resorting to self-help. He noted that such conflicts often affected innocent people who might not even understand the circumstances that triggered the dispute. The chairman further urged residents to cooperate with security personnel deployed to the community, adding that an expanded security meeting had been convened, with youth leaders, the Sarkin Noma and other community leaders from both sides invited to seek a lasting solution. He said anyone who felt unfairly treated or believed their complaints had not received adequate attention should report directly to him for intervention, stressing that grievances must be addressed through lawful channels. Meanwhile, soldiers, police officers, vigilantes and personnel of the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC) have been deployed to the community to restore calm. The FCT Police Command spokesperson, SP Adeh Josephine, did not answer calls seeking the command’s reaction as of the time of filing this report. Not first clash Daily Trust recalls that the latest violence followed an earlier clash on August 11, 2026, across Paikon-Kore, Ibwa and Rafin-Zurfi communities, during which a farmer reportedly lost a hand and three other people sustained machete injuries. Following that incident, Ikwa summoned an emergency security meeting where traditional rulers, community leaders, village and district heads, Ardos of Fulanis, as well as representatives of various security agencies deliberated over the incessant farmers and herders clash. The chairman, at the end of the security meeting, set up a peace and investigative committee. He also carried out on-the-spot assessments of the three affected communities that witnessed cases of farmers and herders clashes. Ikwa promised that the committee’s report would be made public during the stakeholders meeting on Monday (today). Some residents, who spoke to our reporter, said the August 11 incident was a result of cows that allegedly strayed into a farm. They claimed that the tension heightened when the owner of the farm confronted the herders for allowing cows to graze inside his farm, a situation which they said led to a serious confrontation that left four persons injured. Ishaku Danjuma, a farmer, explained that a similar incident also happened in Paiko community on the same day, after some cows allegedly grazed inside a maize farm, resulting in clashes between farmers and herders in the community. He said the farmer queried the herders for allowing cows into the farm, which led to the clash. “If you make your investigations, you will discover that 95 per cent of incidents of farmers and herders clashes across the three communities were as a result of cows straying into people’s farms,” he said. A member of the Paiko community, Usman Yakubu, also said the incessant cases of farmers-herders clash were as a result of cows that allegedly invade farms to destroy crops in the rural communities in the area. He alleged that some herders allowed their cows to eat up some crops, a development he said led to serious confrontations between the affected farmers and the herders across the three communities. “It was as a result of the destruction of some crops which suddenly resulted in a confrontation between the affected farmers and herders, which later led to the injuring of four farmers across three villages,” he said. State of grazing reserves in Abuja The Paikon Kore Grazing Reserve in the Gwagwalada Area Council of the Federal Capital Territory (FCT) is one of the gazetted reserves in Nigeria. The reserve sits on 9,500 hectares of land but most of the area has also been encroached upon by the communities around the area according to herders. In June 2022, a major crisis was averted when the then Minister of Agriculture and Rural Development, Dr Mohammad Mahmood Abubakar visited the reserve to flag off a pasture development programme when youth in the community and the herders started throwing stones at each other. Gbagyi farmers were opposed to the programme, and instead called for the place to be fenced, claiming that pasture development would attract large herdsmen and threaten farms around the reserve. Daily Trust reports that the grazing reserve at Kawu in the Bwari Area Council has not been effectively put into use due to a lack of basic facilities and infrastructure. The grazing reserve, which spans approximately 9,000 hectares, was originally designed to accommodate about 30,000 cattle and 10,000 households. item.title: The one change that worked: I deleted Instagram – and embraced the joys of a truly private life
item.description: I’d become obsessed with appealing to my invisible audience. But since I ditched the app a year ago, my quieter moments have taken on brilliant new meaning I first downloaded Instagram when I was 17 and became hooked on it the way most people fall in love: slowly, and then all at once. For a long time, I never considered myself a social media addict. I self-righteously refused to download TikTok, declared Snapchat to be for “children”, and posted less regularly on Instagram than half of the people I followed. As I went through my university years, however, certain changes crept up on me. I began to swap reading – or essay-writing – for hours spent curating new posts. On my way home from lectures (or later, from my work as a journalist), I would spend ages trying to take the artsiest, most perfect picture of that evening’s sunset for my story – as if the people who followed me were eagerly awaiting yet another photo of one of the Earth’s rotations. What usually followed was a night of reloading my feed to see how many people had reacted to my post – or worse, hadn’t reacted at all. Continue reading...

item.title: Engineer was so sick of office pranks, he 'wiped' his antagonist's disk
item.description: Monday mornings are no joke, so The Register always tries to lighten them up with a new installment of "Who, Me?" – our reader-contributed column that shares your stories of workplace japes, mistakes, and escapes. This week, meet a reader we'll Regomize as "Joe" who told us that while studying for an electrical engineering degree in the late 1990s, he scored a gig in the messaging lab at an Australian mobile carrier. "The office there was full of practical jokers," he wrote. "Boxes of confetti balanced on a door, a bag of prawn heads left under the carpet in one of the senior engineer's cars, hand cream on the phone earpieces... all the usual stuff." Joe told us that one colleague, whom he suggested we call "TF," took the pranks a little too far. "TF liked to sneak up behind me and ROAR in my ear to scare me in the hope I would jump," Joe wrote. "As this was not an especially clever tactic, I resolved to make my revenge a legendary once-and-for-all-time affair." Joe couldn't find an opportunity until his last week in the job, which helpfully coincided with TF attending a conference. "All the PCs had Borland C compilers installed," Joe explained. "I used it to write a completely harmless program that looked exactly like MS-DOS formatting a disk." The program even wrote junk data to a temporary file so the PC's disk activity light would flash, making the fake formatting operation more convincing. After a few minutes of blinkenlights faking the formatting, the program displayed a message revealing the prank. Joe added the program to autoexec.bat so it would run whenever the PC booted, but set it to termintate immediately until a month after his departure. "About five or six weeks later I got a phone call from one of the other guys," Joe recalled. "You're a bloody genius, TF just about shat himself this morning." "Mission accomplished!" Joe declared. By then, he was safely out of the job. Have you pranked your way to revenge? Email Who, Me? and tell us how it went. ®

item.title: ConnectWise turns off its SaaS-y backup, security, and management services to probe security SNAFU
item.description: SaaS-for-managed services providers ConnectWise has initiated a “service interruption” for its some of its offerings after detecting unauthorized access. ConnectWise offers ERP tailored to the needs of managed services providers (MSPs), plus tools they can use to manage their customers’ environments. Cloud Backup is one of those tools and does what it says on the tin for data stored on-prem, in the cloud, or in SaaS services like M365 and Google Workspace. On October 16, the company published an advisory revealing that on the 15th it “identified unauthorized access to application identities within the ConnectWise Cloud Backup environment.” “The service interruption affects partners and customers using Cloud Backup, formerly known as SkyKick. Because SaaS Security and Cloud Management are integrated with Cloud Backup, those services have also been suspended out of an abundance of caution while our investigation and remediation continue,” the company advised. The suspension does not mean MSPs, or their customers, should assume that their environments were compromised, just that ConnectWise isn’t confident it can operate its services safely at this time. As of 16:00 UTC on October 18, the services remain unavailable, which means end-users can’t back up data, access their archives, or restore data. “Existing archives remain encrypted, isolated, and preserved, with no evidence of unauthorized access. Our teams continue monitoring affected environments, conducting forensic analysis and threat hunting, and carrying out remediation activities,” the company’s veep of security operations, Jason Ferguson, wrote on Reddit. ConnectWise has not offered much detail on the incident, other than to publish some indicators of compromise it thinks are tied to a handful of IP addresses and integrations with third-party apps. It has also disabled some integrations between Cloud Backup and Exchange, Teams, SharePoint Online, and its own products. Security outfit Huntress offered a starker view and wrote “A Microsoft 365 credential (API secret) belonging to ConnectWise Cloud Backup has been compromised, and Huntress has confirmed it is being used to gain unauthorized access to customers' M365 environments.” “In one Huntress partner tenant, a second ConnectWise application, ConnectWise Cloud Management - MS Teams (Application ID 24205314-2b89-4e07-a2a4-579e898a5640), gave itself Global Administrator and then added new credentials to two other applications in that tenant, one of them being a single-tenant Huntress application unique to this partner.” “Disabling M365 apps, including the abused ConnectWise apps will not remove credentials that were already added,” the firm warns. “You must review the credentials on all of your M365 applications.” ConnectWise says it “cannot discuss threat actor attribution at this time” because it is focused on “investigation, remediation, and supporting affected partners and their customers.” It has, however, called on its customers to pro
item.content:encoded: SaaS-for-managed services providers ConnectWise has initiated a “service interruption” for its some of its offerings after detecting unauthorized access. ConnectWise offers ERP tailored to the needs of managed services providers (MSPs), plus tools they can use to manage their customers’ environments. Cloud Backup is one of those tools and does what it says on the tin for data stored on-prem, in the cloud, or in SaaS services like M365 and Google Workspace. On October 16, the company published an advisory revealing that on the 15th it “identified unauthorized access to application identities within the ConnectWise Cloud Backup environment.” “The service interruption affects partners and customers using Cloud Backup, formerly known as SkyKick. Because SaaS Security and Cloud Management are integrated with Cloud Backup, those services have also been suspended out of an abundance of caution while our investigation and remediation continue,” the company advised. The suspension does not mean MSPs, or their customers, should assume that their environments were compromised, just that ConnectWise isn’t confident it can operate its services safely at this time. As of 16:00 UTC on October 18, the services remain unavailable, which means end-users can’t back up data, access their archives, or restore data. “Existing archives remain encrypted, isolated, and preserved, with no evidence of unauthorized access. Our teams continue monitoring affected environments, conducting forensic analysis and threat hunting, and carrying out remediation activities,” the company’s veep of security operations, Jason Ferguson, wrote on Reddit. ConnectWise has not offered much detail on the incident, other than to publish some indicators of compromise it thinks are tied to a handful of IP addresses and integrations with third-party apps. It has also disabled some integrations between Cloud Backup and Exchange, Teams, SharePoint Online, and its own products. Security outfit Huntress offered a starker view and wrote “A Microsoft 365 credential (API secret) belonging to ConnectWise Cloud Backup has been compromised, and Huntress has confirmed it is being used to gain unauthorized access to customers' M365 environments.” “In one Huntress partner tenant, a second ConnectWise application, ConnectWise Cloud Management - MS Teams (Application ID 24205314-2b89-4e07-a2a4-579e898a5640), gave itself Global Administrator and then added new credentials to two other applications in that tenant, one of them being a single-tenant Huntress application unique to this partner.” “Disabling M365 apps, including the abused ConnectWise apps will not remove credentials that were already added,” the firm warns. “You must review the credentials on all of your M365 applications.” ConnectWise says it “cannot discuss threat actor attribution at this time” because it is focused on “investigation, remediation, and supporting affected partners and their customers.” It has, however, called on its customers to probe any M365 environments they manage for signs of compromise. This is where things get tricky, because ConnectWise has no knowledge of those setups – as is proper because it is a platform provider and its MSP clients manage end-user relationships. It’s therefore relying on MSPs to do the right thing. MSPs are under no obligation to disclose the platforms they use to deliver their services. Indeed, for some organizations the allure of working with an MSP is to access packaged services they never need to learn or worry about. End-user organizations that may be happily oblivious about ConnectWise’s contribution to their business are therefore in an awkward position. Businesses that serve MSPs are a frequent target for attackers, who see the chance to compromise the likes of ConnectWise as a possible route to crack all of their partners and those service providers' end-users. The 2021 attack on Kaseya is the most notorious example of such an incident. ConnectWise will be hoping it doesn't take the crown. ®

item.title: APOD: 2026 October 19 – Treble Clef: Unusual X-ray Hot Radio Source
item.description: APOD Science APOD APOD: 2026 October 19 –… Today’s APOD Archive Submissions Index Search Calendar RSS Education About Discuss APOD Astronomy Picture of the Day Discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer. Treble Clef: Unusual X-ray Hot Radio Source Explanation: Explanation : What is Treble Clef? This unusual radio structure extends over 2 million light-years and resembles a common musical symbol — but has its visible light hidden by our own Milky Way Galaxy . Examined in 2004, the nature of VLSS J0318.9+5755, dubbed Treble Clef , remained unknown. Recent observations by the Chandra X-ray Observatory and eROSITA , however, have led to the hypothesis that the Treble Clef central cloud of charged particles was originally expelled by a supermassive black hole at the center of a galaxy. After the radio emission from those particles faded, they may have been reinvigorated by a shock wave from the collision of two clusters of galaxies . The featured composite image shows radio emission in red, while recently discovered X-rays are shown in blue. Unusual objects like Treble Clef give humanity unexpected clues about how whole clusters of galaxies interact as well as the general evolution of our universe . item.title: Autumn Paints Poland’s Bieszczady Mountains
item.description: Earth Observatory Science Earth Observatory Autumn Paints Poland’s… Earth Earth Observatory Image of the Day EO Explorer Topics All Topics Atmosphere Land Heat & Radiation Life on Earth Human Dimensions Natural Events Oceans Remote Sensing Technology Snow & Ice Water More Content Collections Global Maps World of Change Articles Earth Matters Blog Blue Marble: Next Generation EO Kids Mission: Biomes About About Us Subscribe 🛜 RSS Contact Us Search As the air grows cooler and days shorter, brown bears prowl the Carpathian Mountains of southern Poland with the goal of fattening up ahead of winter hibernation. In a more conspicuous sign of autumn, beech and other deciduous trees blanketing the hillsides start to sport reds and golds. The seasonal transformation was underway in southeast Poland’s Bieszczady National Park on October 8, 2026, when the OLI (Operational Land Imager) on the NASA-USGS Landsat 9 satellite captured this image. European beech ( Fagus sylvatica ) dominates the area’s forests, with other species such as sycamore maple ( Acer pseudoplatanus ) also contributing to vibrant color in the fall. Dropping air temperatures and waning daylight cause these trees to curtail the production of chlorophyll , the molecule that plants use to synthesize food. Without it, the leaves’ green pigments fade, allowing the yellows and reds of other pigments to show through. A descendent of ice-age survivors, the European beech has persisted across millennia in a range of climates. After the glaciers retreated, beech forests spread northward across the European continent from isolated refugia in the Carpathians, Alps, and other mountain ranges, and played a crucial role in reforesting the previously ice-covered land. Portions of Bieszczady National Park are included within UNESCO’s network of ancient and primeval beech forests spanning 18 countries. Expansive as their footprint across Europe may be, beech forests reach only so high in elevation—about 1,000 to 1,260 meters (3,300 to 4,100 feet)—in this area. Above that is the realm of the polonina , a Slavic term for subalpine meadow, consisting of open grasslands and shrubby thickets of rowan (mountain ash), willows, and green alder. Patches of polonina stretch across ridge tops to the east-southeast of Smerek and appear tan, having lost their summer greenness . The Bieszczady Mountains are renowned not only for forests and mountain meadows but also for charismatic wildlife. European bison, once extinct in the wild , were reintroduced to the area in the 1960s and now roam the hills by the hundreds, according to recent surveys . Additionally, populations of brown bears and Eurasian lynx find refuge and ample food sources in the forests. NASA Earth Observatory image by Michala Garrison, using Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey . Story by Lindsey Doermann. item.content:encoded: Earth Observatory Science Earth Observatory Autumn Paints Poland’s… Earth Earth Observatory Image of the Day EO Explorer Topics All Topics Atmosphere Land Heat & Radiation Life on Earth Human Dimensions Natural Events Oceans Remote Sensing Technology Snow & Ice Water More Content Collections Global Maps World of Change Articles Earth Matters Blog Blue Marble: Next Generation EO Kids Mission: Biomes About About Us Subscribe 🛜 RSS Contact Us Search As the air grows cooler and days shorter, brown bears prowl the Carpathian Mountains of southern Poland with the goal of fattening up ahead of winter hibernation. In a more conspicuous sign of autumn, beech and other deciduous trees blanketing the hillsides start to sport reds and golds. The seasonal transformation was underway in southeast Poland’s Bieszczady National Park on October 8, 2026, when the OLI (Operational Land Imager) on the NASA-USGS Landsat 9 satellite captured this image. European beech ( Fagus sylvatica ) dominates the area’s forests, with other species such as sycamore maple ( Acer pseudoplatanus ) also contributing to vibrant color in the fall. Dropping air temperatures and waning daylight cause these trees to curtail the production of chlorophyll , the molecule that plants use to synthesize food. Without it, the leaves’ green pigments fade, allowing the yellows and reds of other pigments to show through. A descendent of ice-age survivors, the European beech has persisted across millennia in a range of climates. After the glaciers retreated, beech forests spread northward across the European continent from isolated refugia in the Carpathians, Alps, and other mountain ranges, and played a crucial role in reforesting the previously ice-covered land. Portions of Bieszczady National Park are included within UNESCO’s network of ancient and primeval beech forests spanning 18 countries. Expansive as their footprint across Europe may be, beech forests reach only so high in elevation—about 1,000 to 1,260 meters (3,300 to 4,100 feet)—in this area. Above that is the realm of the polonina , a Slavic term for subalpine meadow, consisting of open grasslands and shrubby thickets of rowan (mountain ash), willows, and green alder. Patches of polonina stretch across ridge tops to the east-southeast of Smerek and appear tan, having lost their summer greenness . The Bieszczady Mountains are renowned not only for forests and mountain meadows but also for charismatic wildlife. European bison, once extinct in the wild , were reintroduced to the area in the 1960s and now roam the hills by the hundreds, according to recent surveys . Additionally, populations of brown bears and Eurasian lynx find refuge and ample food sources in the forests. item.title: ICANN vows to work faster, improve transparency
item.description: Internet governance organization the Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers (ICANN) has come to the realization it needs to move faster. The org today opened its annual conference in Bali, Indonesia, with an opening ceremony during which chair Tripti Sinha noted that it’s now just over ten years since the US government effectively handed over internet governance responsibilities from the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) to ICANN. Sinha observed that much has changed online in the last decade, but that despite predictions to the contrary at the time of the handover, ICANN has kept multi-stakeholder internet governance alive and well. “A decade later, the strongest sign of success is what did not happen,” she said. “DNS did not fragment. The coordination of unique identifiers was not destabilized. The internet continues to work.” The chair said ICANN aims to ensure that success continues and said the org must therefore evolve. “If the multi-stakeholder model is to remain credible, we must have the resolve to examine and where necessary enhance the mechanisms through which we hold ourselves accountable,” she said. ICANN last year commenced a “review of reviews” that Sinha said reflects the organization’s willingness to examine its own operations. She thinks that work is necessary in part due to the advent of artificial intelligence, which she predicted will likely create new challenges for management of the resources ICANN tends to. “Agents could reshape DNS traffic patterns and intensify demand on the systems that enable discovery, authentication, and trust online,” she said, adding that AI could both create more malicious DNS registrations and help to defend against them. “ICANN must anticipate change without rushing ahead of evidence, innovating without compromising trust,” she said, calling for the body to deliver “Governance capable of adapting to the speed of emerging risk.” ICANN CEO Kurt Erik Lindqvist touched on similar themes in his speech, calling for the body to improve its ability to support and action community priorities. “Policy development is at the heart of this community,” he said. “Different interests and perspectives have to be heard, tested, and reconsidered. Once the community has done that work ,and recommendations become policy, ICANN has a responsibility to understand what the implementation requires, to make the necessary resources available to sequence the work sensitively, and to be clear about our progress and the choices we are making along the way.” Citing recent successful work on DNS abuse mitigation, Lindqvist said ICANN knows it can nail this process. “That experience showed that we are responding with pace when the objective is clear, responsibilities are understood, and there is alignment around what needs to happen next,” he said. “I would like us to bring that same discipline and rigor to more of our work.” He therefore called for ICANN to be at its best, more often. “There will always b

The International Confederation of Music Publishers (ICMP) – which represents Sony, Warner and Universal as well as thousands of independent publishers on six continents – has warned that of the dozens of countries approached to water down copyright laws, Australia appears to be the only to consider doing so. item.title: Linux KVM guest-host escape rated critical, may represent a new way to attack penguin-powered networking
item.description: Paulos Yibelo, the researcher who in early October claimed to have found a guest-host escape flaw in Linux KVM, the hypervisor used by most hyperscale clouds, has named the flaw PwnEscape and warned it might represent a new way to attack Linux – on top of being a 9.3-rated critical nasty in its own right. Yibelo’s work is now CVE-2026-99999. It is a scary bug because it makes a guest-host escape possible with a few malformed IPv4 packets. Such attacks are a nightmare security scenario because the whole point of virtualization is carving up hardware into isolated “guest” virtual machines that share a “host” server’s resources – without ever being able to see what other guests or the host are doing. Public clouds rely on that isolation remaining impervious. So do private clouds, because if guest/host isolation is violated, an attacker could conceivably access all the VMs on a host or pool of virtualized hardware. Attacks on a host could give an evildoer access to thousands of VMs, plus containers because many developers now run those constructs in a micro-VM to keep them isolated. PwnEscape makes it possible for guests to access the host, by sending a guest malformed IPv4 packets. As explained in a message from Red Hatter Michael S. Tsirkin in the Linux kernel stable tree, ‘If a packet with bad checksum metadata gets into the ipv4 stack, skb_checksum_help can corrupt the network header and cause a bunch of mischief.” Analysis from threat-finding firm SOC Prime details the mischief. “Linux allows network packets to carry metadata indicating where a checksum operation should begin and where its result should be written. This optimization is legitimate and widely used for checksum offloading, but the security problem arises when less-trusted guest-controlled metadata can influence a write after the packet header has already passed earlier validation stages.” “Because the disclosure could be triggered repeatedly, an attacker controlling a guest workload could potentially collect information from a security domain that the virtual machine should not be able to inspect. This represents a direct failure of the guest-host isolation boundary.” Red Hat’s report says the impact can potentially include “arbitrary code execution on the host, a system crash resulting in Denial of Service, or information disclosure of sensitive memory.” A new class of threat Paulos Yibelo, the researcher who found the flaw, thinks he stumbled upon a novel attack. “As far as we know, PwnEscape exposes an entirely new class of attacks in Linux networking: untrusted checksum metadata can rewrite security-sensitive packet fields after the kernel has already validated and acted on them, undermining assumptions across the networking stack far beyond the original VM escape,” he wrote. “The popular mental model is that VM isolation lives in the virtual-machine monitor. Much of it does. But an attacker-controlled workload does not interact only with arch/x86/kvm/. It interacts with a host
item.content:encoded: Paulos Yibelo, the researcher who in early October claimed to have found a guest-host escape flaw in Linux KVM, the hypervisor used by most hyperscale clouds, has named the flaw PwnEscape and warned it might represent a new way to attack Linux – on top of being a 9.3-rated critical nasty in its own right. Yibelo’s work is now CVE-2026-99999. It is a scary bug because it makes a guest-host escape possible with a few malformed IPv4 packets. Such attacks are a nightmare security scenario because the whole point of virtualization is carving up hardware into isolated “guest” virtual machines that share a “host” server’s resources – without ever being able to see what other guests or the host are doing. Public clouds rely on that isolation remaining impervious. So do private clouds, because if guest/host isolation is violated, an attacker could conceivably access all the VMs on a host or pool of virtualized hardware. Attacks on a host could give an evildoer access to thousands of VMs, plus containers because many developers now run those constructs in a micro-VM to keep them isolated. PwnEscape makes it possible for guests to access the host, by sending a guest malformed IPv4 packets. As explained in a message from Red Hatter Michael S. Tsirkin in the Linux kernel stable tree, ‘If a packet with bad checksum metadata gets into the ipv4 stack, skb_checksum_help can corrupt the network header and cause a bunch of mischief.” Analysis from threat-finding firm SOC Prime details the mischief. “Linux allows network packets to carry metadata indicating where a checksum operation should begin and where its result should be written. This optimization is legitimate and widely used for checksum offloading, but the security problem arises when less-trusted guest-controlled metadata can influence a write after the packet header has already passed earlier validation stages.” “Because the disclosure could be triggered repeatedly, an attacker controlling a guest workload could potentially collect information from a security domain that the virtual machine should not be able to inspect. This represents a direct failure of the guest-host isolation boundary.” Red Hat’s report says the impact can potentially include “arbitrary code execution on the host, a system crash resulting in Denial of Service, or information disclosure of sensitive memory.” A new class of threat Paulos Yibelo, the researcher who found the flaw, thinks he stumbled upon a novel attack. “As far as we know, PwnEscape exposes an entirely new class of attacks in Linux networking: untrusted checksum metadata can rewrite security-sensitive packet fields after the kernel has already validated and acted on them, undermining assumptions across the networking stack far beyond the original VM escape,” he wrote. “The popular mental model is that VM isolation lives in the virtual-machine monitor. Much of it does. But an attacker-controlled workload does not interact only with arch/x86/kvm/. It interacts with a host OS full of optimized, highly composable interfaces.” “If the metadata crosses a trust boundary, every deferred consumer has to inherit the right invariants. And if the packet can be transformed after those invariants are checked, the invariants have to remain true in the new representation.” “That is why a bug that looks, at first, like a malformed checksum hint can become a memory disclosure and a guest-to-host escape primitive. The problem was not how difficult IPv4 is to parse. It was that different parts of Linux were allowed to trust different versions of the same packet.” That’s an important observation, because while Linux KVM is widely used, and free, it is part of Linux – a project comprised of over 40 million lines of code. A vendor named Edera, which offers a secure container runtime based on the Xen hypervisor, last week none-too-gently pointed out that’s a big attack surface and that researchers have found seven escape bugs this year alone including Januscape. AWS, which runs its cloud on KVM, says its elastic compute cloud is not at risk. Google Cloud’s method of using KVM means it is probably in the clear, too. Developers have created an upstream fix in the Linux kernel. It’s percolating into major distros like Debian, RHEL, and Ubuntu and hopefully into virtualization products that rely on KVM, such as Nutanix and Proxmox. In the age of AI, miscreants will doubtless quickly explore Yibelo’s discoveries, making PwnScape potentially quite a moment for Linux developers and users. ®

item.title: Time Lords kill leap seconds, before they become the new Y2K bug
item.description: The Time Lords at the General Conference on Weights and Measures (CGPM)* have decided to stop introducing leap seconds, citing the likelihood they could cause problems with internet of things devices – and therefore a Y2K scale remediation effort – as a reason for the change. As The Register reported last week, the CGPM works to harmonize Universal Time – UT1, which boffins calculate using the changing speed of Earth’s rotation – and the Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) standard that humans use to set time. We big-brained hominids can set standards but can’t do much about the fact that the speed of Earth’s rotation is variable. When our planet’s spin slows, the CGPM adds leap seconds so that UT1 and UTC are in synch. In recent years, they have even pondered a negative leap second because Earth’s rotation has sped up a little. Like all good standards orgs, the CGPM conducts years-long debates about its work. The topic of leap seconds has very much been on the agenda in recent years, as they’re increasingly hard to implement now that humanity relies on billions of devices that can usefully share the same timing data but may not easily account for leap seconds. The matter came to a head at last week’s 28th meeting of the CGPM, at which Time Lords voted to end use of leap seconds. The possibility of a negative leap second seems to have been a major factor. “A negative leap second has not previously been applied, and it is considered to pose a high risk of causing anomalies and disruption to critical infrastructures that are largely unprepared,” the Time Lords wrote in a resolution posted after their vote. “The preparation would create, for the industries that rely on time synchronization, a need for financial investment, whose amount is estimated to be similar to their preparations for the millennium bug.” Readers may recall that in the late 1990s, the world spent billions of dollars remediating software that, due to sensible-at-the-time memory-saving measures from the early years of business computing, couldn’t comfortably handle dates after December 31, 1999. Historians now cite the global cost of Y2K remediation at $300-$600 billion. It's widely thought that money was not well-spent. The CGPM also worries about connected devices. The growing influence of IoT (Internet of Things) technologies, dispersed multi-sensor systems, smart grids, and virtual services for contemporary society, creates an increasing risk of malfunction in operation of systems and services with the insertion of any leap second, especially with a negative one,” they wrote. Another concern raised in the resolution is: “The use of different mitigation methods for leap second introductions by global service providers in their server systems, in order to avoid time steps, leads to inconsistency in timing between different systems and in the disseminated time and frequency, which do not conform to the SI unit [the standard second].” The world is home to myriad manufacturers of IoT d
item.content:encoded: The Time Lords at the General Conference on Weights and Measures (CGPM)* have decided to stop introducing leap seconds, citing the likelihood they could cause problems with internet of things devices – and therefore a Y2K scale remediation effort – as a reason for the change. As The Register reported last week, the CGPM works to harmonize Universal Time – UT1, which boffins calculate using the changing speed of Earth’s rotation – and the Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) standard that humans use to set time. We big-brained hominids can set standards but can’t do much about the fact that the speed of Earth’s rotation is variable. When our planet’s spin slows, the CGPM adds leap seconds so that UT1 and UTC are in synch. In recent years, they have even pondered a negative leap second because Earth’s rotation has sped up a little. Like all good standards orgs, the CGPM conducts years-long debates about its work. The topic of leap seconds has very much been on the agenda in recent years, as they’re increasingly hard to implement now that humanity relies on billions of devices that can usefully share the same timing data but may not easily account for leap seconds. The matter came to a head at last week’s 28th meeting of the CGPM, at which Time Lords voted to end use of leap seconds. The possibility of a negative leap second seems to have been a major factor. “A negative leap second has not previously been applied, and it is considered to pose a high risk of causing anomalies and disruption to critical infrastructures that are largely unprepared,” the Time Lords wrote in a resolution posted after their vote. “The preparation would create, for the industries that rely on time synchronization, a need for financial investment, whose amount is estimated to be similar to their preparations for the millennium bug.” Readers may recall that in the late 1990s, the world spent billions of dollars remediating software that, due to sensible-at-the-time memory-saving measures from the early years of business computing, couldn’t comfortably handle dates after December 31, 1999. Historians now cite the global cost of Y2K remediation at $300-$600 billion. It's widely thought that money was not well-spent. The CGPM also worries about connected devices. The growing influence of IoT (Internet of Things) technologies, dispersed multi-sensor systems, smart grids, and virtual services for contemporary society, creates an increasing risk of malfunction in operation of systems and services with the insertion of any leap second, especially with a negative one,” they wrote. Another concern raised in the resolution is: “The use of different mitigation methods for leap second introductions by global service providers in their server systems, in order to avoid time steps, leads to inconsistency in timing between different systems and in the disseminated time and frequency, which do not conform to the SI unit [the standard second].” The world is home to myriad manufacturers of IoT devices, but fewer standards on how they should behave. Some manufacturers therefore build shabbily insecure devices that ship with vulnerable software that allow them to be subverted with malware, or without facilities that allow easy updates. Billions of devices could therefore fail to implement a leap second. That would become a problem because digital certificates include a notbefore value – a time before which the cert won’t be accepted. Many systems that see a misbehaving cert would reject it. It’s therefore conceivable that if a major ISP’s modems could not accommodate a leap second, the extra sliver of time’s introduction could see the carrier’s network decide its own customers are not trustworthy enough to connect. Scenarios like that rather suggest Time Lords have taken a sensibly long view regarding the perhaps-inevitable fallibility of software developers. The CGPM's replacement for leap seconds is to allow UT1 and UTC to diverge by up to 3,600 seconds under a scheme called "Continuous UTC" that comes into force next year. Humanity has lots of practice adding and removing hours thanks to Daylight Saving time, which some want to sunset. ® * The organisation’s formal name is the Conférence générale des poids et mesures, which yields the initialism CGPM

item.title: Elite-level incompetence is Manchester United’s problem – not Michael Carrick | Barney Ronay
item.description: Getting rid of head coach is not going to solve the problems that led to his appointment. Perhaps it’s worth, for once, doing something different At the final whistle at Elland Road the TV cameras cut to a lingering shot of the Manchester United chief executive, Omar Berrada, looking down pensively from the stands, deciding, it is to be hoped, on a little clemency, a re-sheathing of the managerial shotgun. Here we have the man who hired the man. The man who fires the man. The man who also hired or rehired the previous two men he had to fire. Berrada was poached from Manchester City on the basis of his ability to grow commercial revenue (yes, OK, stop laughing), and appears, like everyone else with any actual reach around here, to exist in a strangely consequence-free bubble. Continue reading...

item.title: Another unremarkable win shows Arsenal’s strength is in depth rather than creativity | Jonathan Wilson
item.description: Champions so risk-averse Forest were lured into thinking they had a chance, until bench was used to see them off Pass. Pass. Pass. Pass. Sideways. Square. Backwards. Pass. Pass. Recycle. Pass. It wasn’t much of a spectacle. But in the end, for the second week running, thanks in no small part of their bench, Arsenal won. Fireworks in the autumn are for Bonfire Night; titles require relentless accumulation. Since the international break, Arsenal have won three games out of three despite not being in the lead at half-time in any of them. Hammered at Brighton and having endured a drab first hour at home to Leeds last week, there has been a rare sense, for the first time really since Manchester City dropped points at Everton at the beginning of May, of Arsenal not being quite at their best, needing to reassert their quality. This was not a performance that would terrify any opponent, but it did highlight Arsenal’s consistency and it did demonstrate just how deep their squad now runs. Continue reading...
